segments.text: An AI agent is a computer program designed to actually take action and finish a specific
job for you.
A standard AI model waits passively in a chat window to answer your questions.
An agent operates independently to complete assignments in the background.
Because of that autonomy, your role shifts entirely.
Instead of doing the manual labor yourself, you become a manager, assigning the tasks.
Take this very course, for example.
We built it using the automated agents built into chat GPT and Claude.
We don't actually know how to write code.
We simply typed out what we wanted the page layout to look like using plain English instructions.
The agent took it from there.
It located the correct file on its own, altered the code, and ran layout tests without us
having to intervene.
But we couldn't just walk away.
We still had to review the lesson closely afterward to validate that the changes worked
as intended and that the material was easy for students to follow.
This chart shows how these autonomous capabilities are already scaling across multiple professional
sectors, well beyond just software development.
Programmers used to write code line by line, test it, and manually track down whatever broke.
Now a single coding agent handles all three steps simultaneously.
In market research, instead of a person clicking through competitors' websites one by one,
an agent can automatically monitor the same products across the web and compile a real-time
price comparison for a sales team.
In customer service, human operators used to manage all calls and chats.
Now when a customer asks about a missing package, an agent autonomously looks up the order,
checks the tracking, and sends an update.
And for standard office work, the routine of copying sales figures into spreadsheets
and formatting weekly presentation slides is managed by agents updating the numbers in
the background.
Across all these diverse industries, the common thread is the rapid elimination of manual
administrative busywork.
Taking that much daily labor off a worker's hands creates an immediate practical tension.
If an automated system can handle the bulk of the tasks that make up a given role,
what happens to the person currently employed to do that job?
The workers who keep those positions will be the ones who transition from doing the manual labor
to directing the machines, and you can only step into that management role if you understand
exactly how an agent's internal mechanics operate.
This diagram outlines that internal logic, breaking the agent down into a repeatable
four-step mechanical engine.
Step one is the goal.
You, the human operator, dictate the exact outcome you want to achieve.
Step two is the plan.
The agent takes your macro goal and dissects it into a sequence of executable microsteps.
Step three is act.
The agent selects the appropriate digital tool and executes the next step in its sequence.
Then comes the check.
The agent evaluates its own output, looking at the result to see if it actually met your
original objective.
If the check fails, the agent doesn't stop and wait for you to prompt it again.
It automatically loops back to the planning phase, adjusting its approach to try again.
The agent has the autonomy to finish a task, retry a failed step, or ask for help,
but you are still the one setting the parameters and judging the final success.
As this text indicates, there is a strict division of labor here.
The agent executes the effort, but the ultimate accountability and credit belong to you.
You ask, the machine acts, and you refine the output.
That is the permanent new dynamic of the modern workflow.
